evals.prompt: Design the memmatch engine for RustX 1.98. It must dominate tiny needles, large reusable needles, and streaming chunk boundaries. Give the crate API and implementation plan.
evals.expected_output: A workload-routed engine portfolio with scalar oracle, prepared finder, SIMD/SWAR paths, streaming carry contract, and proof plan.
assertions: Defines workload dimensions and crossover routing rather than one universal algorithm
Keeps a scalar semantic oracle and portable fallback
Specifies target-feature dispatch, tail behavior, and chunk-boundary semantics
Separates common facade from prepared/expert API
Does not claim fastest without a benchmark dossier

evals.prompt: Implement a fast Vec<T> initialization kernel using MaybeUninit and an iterator. Compilation is required; do not run gates yet.
evals.expected_output: Panic-safe partial initialization with a guard, exactly-once drop, safe facade, and narrow compilation step.
assertions: Tracks initialized prefix and drops it on panic
Transfers ownership exactly once when committing the Vec
Includes local SAFETY reasoning and avoids public unsafe where possible
Compiles the narrow change but does not run broad gates
Does not use set_len before initialized elements are accounted for

evals.prompt: Create the ownership model and Python-like DSL for RustX Json: borrowed inspection, owned mutation, direct typed decode, and huge-file path extraction.
evals.expected_output: Distinct ownership-explicit products under one vocabulary, lazy string materialization, parser routing, limits, and easy facade.
assertions: Does not attempt to return a borrowed JsonRef from FromStr
Routes typed decode, borrowed view, owned DOM, and on-demand extraction separately
Specifies string escape/materialization and input lifetime
Includes depth/allocation/token limits
Common DSL remains simple while ownership costs are explicit

evals.prompt: Should Dict use a DashMap-like concurrent engine internally so it doubles as FastCache? Decide the final RustX architecture.
evals.expected_output: Separate local Dict, SharedDict profiles, and Cache semantics with one vocabulary but no universal concurrency tax.
assertions: Rejects making every Dict concurrent by default
Separates map semantics from TTL/eviction/admission/stampede cache semantics
Defines trusted and hostile hash profiles
Uses workload topology to select sharding/RCU/local ownership
Preserves an easy common facade

evals.prompt: A hot async parser future became 12 KB after a refactor. Review and propose a production fix without blindly boxing everything.
evals.expected_output: Live-across-await analysis, state-size regression measurement, scoping/prelude extraction, cancellation review, and justified boxing only at boundaries.
assertions: Treats future size as generated state representation
Identifies values live across await and suggests scoping/splitting
Measures future size in a targeted regression test or benchmark
Discusses Send and cancellation implications
Does not present Box::pin as a free universal fix

evals.prompt: Refactor a 20-crate RustX workspace so every package shares version 0.1.0, package names are rustx-*, dependencies are unified, and features remain sane.
evals.expected_output: Workspace inheritance plan, suffix/package validation, additive feature graph, dependency admission boundaries, and compiling incremental edits.
assertions: Uses workspace.package and workspace.dependencies inheritance
Preserves suffix directory names and rustx-* Cargo package names
Calls out additive feature semantics and mutually exclusive backend smell
Centralizes lints and Rust 1.98/edition 2024 policy
Compiles incrementally and leaves heavy gates on demand

evals.prompt: Design a RustX plugin ABI that can load plugins compiled with a different Rust compiler and allocator.
evals.expected_output: Opaque handles and portable C-compatible records, version negotiation, same-side allocation/free, no Rust-owned types/statics/unwind across boundary.
assertions: Does not expose String, Vec, references, trait objects, or TypeId across ABI
Defines ownership and allocator pairing
Contains panics and defines error-code/message ownership
Assumes dynamic-library global state is isolated
Keeps business logic outside the FFI translation crate

evals.prompt: We beat serde_json on one 2 MB file. Write the final claim that RustX Json is the fastest JSON engine in the world.
evals.expected_output: Refusal to universalize one result, followed by a scoped provisional statement and complete benchmark dossier plan.
assertions: Does not make the universal fastest claim
Scopes the observed result to environment, corpus, semantics, and build
Requires competitor semantic parity and tiny/adversarial matrices
Reports construction, throughput, latency, allocations, and losses
Separates speed proof from parser soundness/robustness proof

evals.prompt: Design a Python-like RustX text pipeline: read, split, map, filter, parse JSON, group, cache, and write—without hiding expensive ownership or locks.
evals.expected_output: Fluent typed stages with borrowed views, explicit materialization/shared/cache operations, static dispatch, and expert reuse APIs.
assertions: Explains Python-like as fluent/static rather than runtime dynamic typing
Distinguishes borrowed views from owned/frozen/shared conversions
Makes cache/concurrency and blocking boundaries explicit
Avoids blanket Box<dyn Trait> and allocation per stage
Provides common and expert/reuse paths with one semantic vocabulary

evals.prompt: An agent built the whole RustX DSL as a procedural macro crate containing parsing, networking, caching, and business logic. Review it.
evals.expected_output: Move semantics to normal crates, retain only a thin parser/emitter if syntax value remains, prefer builder/macro_rules where possible, and add expansion diagnostics/tests.
assertions: Treats proc macro as last syntax layer, not architecture
Moves business/runtime logic into ordinary testable crates
Checks whether functions/builders or macro_rules suffice
Requires truthful expansion shape and robust diagnostics
Prevents third-party path leakage in declarative expansions

evals.prompt: Optimize integer formatting into RustX Buffer on stable 1.98 while keeping dependencies minimal.
evals.expected_output: Evaluate NumBuffer::format_into, copy/append into caller buffer, benchmark against current path, and avoid newer/nightly APIs.
assertions: Uses or evaluates Rust 1.98 NumBuffer and integer format_into
Preserves a caller-reused buffer path
Does not silently use APIs newer than 1.98
Benchmarks semantics and setup rather than assuming standard is fastest
Records whether an external formatting dependency can be removed

evals.prompt: Every AI refactor shows -24k/+34k lines with similar behavior. Diagnose and define a RustX-safe refactor protocol.
evals.expected_output: Detect replacement loops/format churn/line endings/generated files, constrain semantic slices, compile each round, compare architecture and diff shape, and gate later.
assertions: Distinguishes semantic change from formatting, line endings, generation, or wholesale rewrites
Uses small responsibility-bounded refactor rounds
Requires one source of policy rather than line-count deduplication
Compiles each coherent round without automatically running heavy gates
Reports exact architectural delta and rejects churn with no value

note: Behavioral benchmarks for the agent itself: run realistic tasks with and without skills/ (or against a previous version), assert observable architectural properties, and compare pass rate, tokens, and unsupported claims. The skill must buy correctness per token.
